entries.label: Treats an ordered pair like an unordered set
entries.description: The student thinks (a, b) is the same as (b, a), or the same as {a, b}, so they match components in the wrong positions.

refutation.text_md: You are treating the pair like a set, where only the numbers matter and the order does not. That is true for $\{a, b\}$, but not for an ordered pair $(a, b)$.

In an ordered pair, position carries meaning: the first place is the first projection and the second place is the second projection. Two ordered pairs are equal only when the first projections are equal and the second projections are equal.
Test it on $(a-2, b+1)=(2, -3)$. If you match crosswise, $a-2=-3$ and $b+1=2$ give $a=-1$ and $b=1$. Put these back: the left side is $(-3, 2)$, which is not $(2, -3)$.
Match by position. First projections: $a-2=2$, so $a=4$. Second projections: $b+1=-3$, so $b=-4$. Check: $(4-2,\,-4+1)=(2,-3)$.
Each time, first compare the two first places, then the two second places. Write one equation for each place.

flags.text: The two remarks (order matters; a pair is not a set) were merged into one entry because both lead to the same wrong matching of components. A reviewer may prefer to split them.
I used 'first projection' and 'second projection', as the drill solutions do.

entries.label: Treats X×Y and Y×X as the same
entries.description: The student writes the pairs with the elements in the wrong order, or assumes X×Y gives the same set as Y×X.

refutation.text_md: You have the right pairs of elements in mind, but you treated a pair like a set where order does not matter. In $X\times Y$ the first element of each pair must come from $X$ and the second from $Y$.
Take $X=\{a, b\}$ and $Y=\{-1, 0, 3\}$. Then $X\times Y$ contains $(a, -1)$, but $Y\times X$ contains $(-1, a)$. These are different ordered pairs, so $X\times Y\neq Y\times X$ when $X\neq Y$.

The same thing happens with $Y\times Z$ where $Y=\{4, 0\}$ and $Z=\{4, 5, -2\}$. The answer has pairs like $(4, 5)$ with a $Y$ element first. Writing $(5, 4)$ would put a $Z$ element first, and that belongs to $Z\times Y$.
Before you write each pair, check the order of the product. Take each element of the first set in turn and pair it with every element of the second set, always writing the first set's element first.

entries.label: Adds the sizes instead of multiplying
entries.description: To find n(X×Y) or n(X²), the student adds (or doubles) the numbers of elements instead of multiplying n(X) by n(Y).
entries.signal: n(X×Z) = 5 instead of 6; n(Z²) = 6 instead of 9; n(Y²) = 4 by coincidence

refutation.text_md: You found the right sizes, $n(Z)=3$, but then combined them by adding. Adding counts the elements of two sets put together. A cartesian product counts pairs.

Look at $Z^2$ with $Z=\{4, 5, -2\}$. Pair $4$ with each of the 3 elements, then pair $5$ with each of the 3, then $-2$ with each of the 3. That gives 3 groups of 3 pairs, which is $3\times 3=9$ pairs, not $3+3=6$.
The same applies to $X\times Z$ with $X=\{2, -1\}$ and $Z=\{4, 5, -2\}$. Each of the 2 elements of $X$ is paired with 3 elements of $Z$, so there are $2\times 3=6$ pairs, not $2+3=5$.
Use $n(X\times Y)=n(X)\times n(Y)$, and for a square $n(X^2)=n(X)\times n(X)$. A check is that $n(Y^2)=2\times 2=4$ for $Y=\{4, 0\}$ happens to equal $2+2$, so test your method on $Z^2$ as well.

flags.text: Used 'ordered pairs' and 'cartesian product' as in the book's solutions; 'first set / second set' is my own plain wording.
No source directly evidences the adding error; it rests on the n×n remark. The book's worked example for Y×X prints (3, 0) where (3, a) is meant; not used in student text.

entries.label: X × Y treated as the same as Y × X
entries.description: Assumes the Cartesian product is commutative, so the pairs come out reversed.
entries.signal: Every pair in the answer is a pair of the correct answer with its components swapped.

refutation.text_md: You built every pair the product contains — the pairing is right.
But in $X \times Y$ the FIRST component always comes from $X$. With $X = \{1, 2\}$ and $Y = \{5\}$ that gives $\{(1,5), (2,5)\}$.
$Y \times X$ would give $\{(5,1), (5,2)\}$ — the same elements, a different set.
Read the product left to right: first set supplies the first component.

entries.label: Cartesian product confused with the union
entries.description: Lists the elements of both sets instead of forming ordered pairs.
entries.signal: The answer is a set of single elements rather than a set of pairs.

refutation.text_md: The elements you listed are the right ones to be working with.
But $X \times Y$ is a set of ORDERED PAIRS, not a set of elements: each pair takes one element from $X$ and one from $Y$.

entries.label: Arrows drawn from the second set
entries.description: Starts each arrow in an arrow diagram from an element of Y rather than of X.
entries.signal: The diagram or the reasoning reverses the direction of every arrow.

refutation.text_md: You know the diagram joins one set to the other — that is the idea.
In the arrow diagram of $X \times Y$ every arrow STARTS at an element of $X$, the first projection, and ends at an element of $Y$.
The direction carries the order of the pair; reversing it draws $Y \times X$ instead.

entries.label: Total points read as the number of columns
entries.description: Reports the whole point count of a net diagram where a column count is asked.
entries.signal: The answer equals n(X) x n(Y) rather than one of the factors.

refutation.text_md: That number is genuinely in the diagram — it is the total of the points.
Each COLUMN holds $n(Y)$ points, so the number of columns is the total divided by the height.
$15$ points in columns of $3$ gives $5$ columns.

entries.label: Cardinalities added instead of multiplied
entries.description: Computes n(X) + n(Y) where n(X) x n(Y) is required.
entries.signal: The answer is the sum of the two set sizes.

refutation.text_md: You are combining the two sizes, which is the right shape of answer.
Every element of $X$ pairs with EVERY element of $Y$, so the count multiplies: $n(X \times Y) = n(X) \times n(Y)$.
Adding would count each element once instead of pairing them.

entries.label: Components subtracted instead of added
entries.description: Reaches the right pair of values but subtracts them.
entries.signal: The answer equals the difference of the two components.

refutation.text_md: Your values are right: $a = 3$ and $b = 5$.
The question asks for $a + b = 8$; $2$ is $b - a$.
The equality of ordered pairs gives you the two numbers. What you do with them afterwards is whatever the question asks for.

entries.label: Values written side by side instead of combined
entries.description: Writes the two components as digits of one number rather than performing the operation.
entries.signal: The answer is the two component values concatenated.

refutation.text_md: You found $a = 3$ and $b = 5$ correctly.
Writing them next to each other gives $35$, which is a new number, not a sum.
$a + b$ means add: $3 + 5 = 8$.

entries.label: Components multiplied when the question asks for their sum
entries.description: Finds a and b correctly from the equal pairs, then combines them with the wrong operation.
entries.signal: The answer equals a x b where a + b was asked, or the reverse.

refutation.text_md: You read the pair correctly — that is the hard part, and you did it.
From $(a, 5) = (3, b)$ the like components match: $a = 3$ and $b = 5$.
The question then asks for $a + b$, which is $8$. The answer $15$ is $a \times b$.
Worth a habit: once you have the two values, read the last line of the question again before you combine them.

entries.label: Order of the pair ignored
entries.description: Reports (b, a) where (a, b) was asked; treats an ordered pair as an unordered set.
entries.signal: The answer is the correct pair with its components swapped.

refutation.text_md: Both of your numbers are right — the issue is which one goes first.
An ordered pair is *ordered*: $(0, 2)$ and $(2, 0)$ name different points and are not equal unless the two components happen to be the same.
Match first-with-first and second-with-second, and keep them in that order when you write the answer.

entries.label: Sign lost when moving a term across the equals sign
entries.description: Solves x − 4 = 9 as x = 9 − 4, or y + 2 = 7 as y = 7 + 2.
entries.signal: The answer differs from the correct one by twice the transposed term.

refutation.text_md: Transposing is the right move — the sign is what flips.
Whatever is SUBTRACTED on one side is ADDED on the other: $x - 4 = 9$ gives $x = 9 + 4 = 13$.
And the reverse: $y + 2 = 7$ gives $y = 7 - 2 = 5$.
Check by substituting back into the original equation — it costs five seconds and catches every sign slip.

entries.label: A point on an axis placed in a quadrant
entries.description: Assigns a point with a zero coordinate to a quadrant; the axes belong to none.
entries.signal: A point containing 0 is reported as being in a quadrant.

refutation.text_md: The sign you did read is right.
But $(0, -3)$ has a zero first coordinate, so it sits ON the $y$-axis rather than inside any quadrant.
The axes divide the plane into the four quadrants and belong to none of them — a zero anywhere in the pair puts the point on an axis.

entries.label: Quadrant chosen from one coordinate
entries.description: Names the quadrant from the sign of x without checking y, or the reverse.
entries.signal: The named quadrant matches one coordinate's sign and contradicts the other.

refutation.text_md: You are reading signs, which is exactly the right instinct.
A quadrant needs BOTH signs: $(-2, 5)$ is negative then positive, which is the second quadrant.
In order: $(+,+)$ first, $(-,+)$ second, $(-,-)$ third, $(+,-)$ fourth.

entries.label: A relation taken to be a subset of one of the sets
entries.description: Treats a relation as a set of elements rather than a set of ordered pairs.
entries.signal: The answer names X or Y where X x Y is required.

refutation.text_md: A relation does involve both sets — that part is right.
But its members are ORDERED PAIRS, so a relation from $X$ to $Y$ is a subset of $X \times Y$.
$X$ alone holds single elements, and a pair cannot be an element of it.

entries.label: The rule of the relation applied in reverse
entries.description: Reads a R b as b R a, producing every pair the wrong way round.
entries.signal: Each pair in the answer is a correct pair reversed.

refutation.text_md: You applied the rule to every element, which is the method.
The rule $b = 2a$ takes $a$ from $X$ first: $a = 1$ gives $b = 2$, so the pair is $(1, 2)$.
Writing $(2, 1)$ answers a different question — the relation 'is half of' rather than 'is double of'.
Say the rule aloud in the order the pair is written and it stays straight.

entries.label: a divides b read as b divides a
entries.description: Reverses the direction of the divisibility relation, which is not symmetric.
entries.signal: The pairs given are the correct pairs with their order reversed.

refutation.text_md: You found the right numbers to pair. What needs checking is which one comes first.
In $a\,R\,b$, the first element divides the second: $(2, 4)$ belongs to the relation because $2$ divides $4$.
Turning a pair round changes what it says: $(4, 2)$ would claim that $4$ divides $2$, which is false. Divisibility works in one direction only.
Read every pair left to right as "first divides second", and keep only the pairs where that is true.

entries.label: A relation on X taken to be a subset of X
entries.description: Treats a relation on a set as a set of elements rather than of ordered pairs.
entries.signal: The answer names X, or a set of single elements.

refutation.text_md: A relation on $X$ does live entirely inside $X$'s world — that instinct is right.
Its members are ORDERED PAIRS of elements of $X$, so $R \subseteq X \times X$.
$X$ itself holds single elements, and a pair is not one of them.

entries.label: Pairs of an element with itself left out
entries.description: Omits (x, x) from a relation on a set, assuming a relation must join two different elements.
entries.signal: The answer is the correct relation minus its self-paired members.

refutation.text_md: Every pair you listed genuinely satisfies the rule.
One is missing: with $a + b = 0$ and $a = b = 0$, the pair $(0, 0)$ satisfies it too.
A relation on a set may pair an element with itself — nothing in the definition forbids it.

entries.label: An element of the domain left without an image
entries.description: Accepts a relation as a function although some element of X never appears.
entries.signal: The chosen relation has fewer pairs than n(X).

refutation.text_md: No element is doubled here, which is half the condition.
The other half is that EVERY element of $X$ must appear. With $X = \{1,2,3\}$ and only $(1,2), (2,3)$, the element $3$ has no image.
Count the pairs against $n(X)$: for a function on $X$ they must match.

entries.label: An element of the domain given two images
entries.description: Accepts a relation as a function although one first projection appears twice.
entries.signal: The chosen relation contains two pairs sharing a first component.

refutation.text_md: Every pair there is legal on its own.
But $1$ appears as a first projection twice, in $(1,2)$ and $(1,3)$, so $1$ has two images.
A function gives each input exactly one output — one repeat is enough to disqualify it.

entries.label: A graph drawn with two outputs for one input
entries.description: Sketches a curve that doubles back, treating any drawn line as the graph of a function.
entries.signal: At some $x$ the drawn curve carries two different $y$ values.

refutation.text_md: That is a perfectly good curve — it is just not the graph of a function.
A function gives each input EXACTLY ONE output. Your sketch doubles back, so there is an $x$ with two different $y$ values, and the rule cannot say which one it means.
That is what the vertical line test checks: slide a vertical line across, and if it ever crosses your curve twice, the relation is not a function.
It is the same condition from the start of the year, seen from the side: a relation is a function when no input is used twice.

entries.label: The function condition applied to the second set
entries.description: Requires each element of Y to appear once, instead of each element of X appearing exactly once as a first projection.
entries.signal: The stated condition is about images rather than about the domain.

refutation.text_md: You have the right shape of condition — 'exactly once' is the key phrase.
It applies to the FIRST set: every element of $X$ must appear exactly once as a first projection.
Elements of $Y$ may repeat, or not appear at all — that is why the range can be a proper subset of the codomain.

entries.label: Range and codomain treated as the same set
entries.description: Reports the whole codomain as the range; the range is the set of images actually reached.
entries.signal: The answer is Y rather than the set of second components of f.

refutation.text_md: You have found the right set to be looking at — $Y$ is where the images live.
The RANGE is only the part of $Y$ that is actually reached: the second components of the pairs, $\{3, 5, 7\}$.
$2$ belongs to the codomain but is nobody's image, so it is not in the range.
Range $\subseteq$ codomain, and the two are equal only when every element of $Y$ gets used.

entries.label: Range confused with the domain
entries.description: Gives the set of inputs where the set of images was asked.
entries.signal: The answer is X rather than the images.

refutation.text_md: That set is the domain — the inputs.
The range is what comes OUT: the second component of each pair, $\{3, 5, 7\}$.
Domain in, range out; the arrow diagram runs left to right.

entries.label: Counts 1/x or √x terms as allowed in a polynomial
entries.description: The student sees a sum of x-terms and numbers and calls it a polynomial without checking that every power of x is a whole number.

refutation.text_md: You noticed that the function is built from $x$ and numbers added together, and that is a good start. A polynomial needs one more thing: every power of $x$ must be a whole number.
Rewrite each term as a power of $x$. In $x^3+\frac{1}{x}+7$, the term $\frac{1}{x}$ is $x^{-1}$, and in $x^2+\sqrt{x}+8$, the term $\sqrt{x}$ is $x^{\frac{1}{2}}$.

The powers $-1$ and $\frac{1}{2}$ are not whole numbers, so these two functions do not fit the form $a_0+a_1x+\dots+a_nx^n$. Neither is a polynomial. Compare $x^3+x^2+3$, whose powers are $3$, $2$ and $0$, all whole numbers, so it is a polynomial.
Next time, write every term as $x^{\text{power}}$ and check each power. If any one is negative or a fraction, the answer is No.

entries.label: Reads the degree from the unexpanded rule
entries.description: The student takes the degree from the powers they see in the brackets or in the first terms, instead of expanding and simplifying first.
entries.signal: Gives 2 for x^2-(x^2-3), or 2 for x(x-2x^2).

refutation.text_md: You looked at the powers of $x$ that are printed and picked the biggest. That works when the rule is already written as $a_0+a_1x+\dots+a_nx^n$, but brackets can hide what is left.
Take $f(x)=x^2-(x^2-3)$. Reading it as it stands suggests degree $2$. Remove the brackets: $x^2-x^2+3$. The $x^2$ terms cancel, so $f(x)=3$, which has no $x$ term. The degree is $0$, not $2$.
Take $f(x)=x(x-2x^2)$. The brackets show $x^2$, but multiplying out gives $x^2-2x^3$. The highest power is $3$, so the degree is $3$.
Next time, expand and simplify first, then read off the highest power of $x$ that is still there.

entries.label: Degree read off without expanding
entries.description: Takes the highest power visible in the unexpanded form instead of multiplying out first.
entries.signal: The reported degree is the largest exponent appearing in the brackets.

refutation.text_md: You are looking for the highest power, which is the right definition.
It has to be the highest power AFTER multiplying out: $x(x - 2x^2) = x^2 - 2x^3$, so the degree is $3$.
Expand first, then read the degree.

entries.label: An expression with a negative or fractional power called a polynomial
entries.description: Accepts 1/x or √x inside a polynomial function.
entries.signal: The chosen function contains a variable in a denominator or under a root.

refutation.text_md: Most of that expression IS polynomial — the $x^3$ and the constant are fine.
A polynomial function allows only whole-number powers of $x$, so $\frac{1}{x}$ (which is $x^{-1}$) and $\sqrt{x}$ (which is $x^{1/2}$) both disqualify it.
Check every term: any $x$ in a denominator or under a root means it is not a polynomial.

entries.label: Thinks every straight-line graph passes through (0, 0)
entries.description: The student carries the rule for f(x) = ax over to every linear function, so they force the line through the origin even when the rule has a constant term such as −3.

refutation.text_md: You remembered that the graph of $f(x)=ax$ is a straight line through the origin $(0,0)$. That is true, and it is a good fact to hold on to. The question is whether it covers every linear function.
That fact is only about functions of the form $f(x)=ax$, with nothing added or subtracted. $f(x)=2x-3$ has a $-3$ as well, so it is a different kind of rule.
Test it by finding $f(0)$. $f(0)=2(0)-3=-3$. The point on the graph with $x=0$ is $(0,-3)$, not $(0,0)$. A line through the origin would need $f(0)=0$, and here it isn't.
The other points agree: $f(1)=2-3=-1$ and $f(2)=4-3=1$. These give $(1,-1)$ and $(2,1)$. None of the three points is the origin, so the line cannot pass through $(0,0)$.
Don't decide where the line goes in advance. Calculate $f(0)$, $f(1)$ and $f(2)$, write the ordered pairs in a table, plot them, and draw the straight line through the points you plotted.

entries.label: Constant function drawn as a vertical line
entries.description: Takes f(x) = c to be parallel to the y-axis rather than the x-axis.
entries.signal: The answer names the y-axis where the x-axis is correct.

refutation.text_md: You know the graph is a line parallel to an axis — that is the right picture.
$f(x) = 5$ means the output is $5$ for EVERY input, so the height never changes: a horizontal line, parallel to the $x$-axis.
A vertical line would give one input many outputs, which cannot be a function at all.

entries.label: Constant function taken to mean the function is zero
entries.description: Reads 'constant' as 'equal to zero' rather than 'unchanging'.
entries.signal: The answer sets the whole function, rather than the coefficient of x, to zero.

refutation.text_md: You are right that something has to be zero — it is the coefficient of $x$, not the function.
Constant means the output never CHANGES, whatever $x$ is. $f(x) = 5$ is constant and never zero.
So in $f(x) = (m-3)x + 5$ the condition is $m - 3 = 0$, which leaves $f(x) = 5$.

entries.label: The sign of the gradient not read as the line's direction
entries.description: Sketches $y = mx + c$ leaning the wrong way, treating the sign of $m$ as affecting only where the line sits rather than which way it goes.
entries.signal: The drawn line rises where it should fall, or the reverse.

refutation.text_md: Your line is straight and it crosses the axis in the right place — the shape and the intercept are both right.
The sign of $m$ says which way it goes: $m > 0$ rises to the right, $m < 0$ falls.
So $y = -x + 2$ starts at $2$ on the $y$-axis and goes DOWN one for every step right.
Read the sign of $m$ before drawing, and the direction is settled before you start.

entries.label: Slope and y-intercept exchanged
entries.description: Reads b as the slope and a as the intercept in f(x) = ax + b.
entries.signal: The two values appear in each other's roles.

refutation.text_md: Both numbers are the right ones to be using.
In $f(x) = ax + b$ the number ATTACHED TO $x$ is the slope; the loose number is the $y$-intercept.
Substituting $x = 0$ settles it: $f(0) = b$, so $b$ is where the line crosses the $y$-axis.

entries.label: f(x) = ax assumed to cut the y-axis at a
entries.description: Confuses the coefficient with an intercept, so the line is thought to pass through (0, a).
entries.signal: The named fixed point is (0, a) or (a, 0) rather than the origin.

refutation.text_md: You are right that the line has a fixed point regardless of $a$.
Substitute $x = 0$: $f(0) = a \times 0 = 0$, so the line passes through $(0,0)$, the origin.
In $f(x) = ax + b$ the intercept is $b$; here $b = 0$, which is exactly what puts the line through the origin.

entries.label: Point tested with its coordinates the wrong way round
entries.description: Substitutes the y-value for x when checking whether a point lies on a line.
entries.signal: The rejected/accepted point is the correct one reversed.

refutation.text_md: Your substitution method is right — that is how you test a point.
Substitute the FIRST coordinate for $x$: for $(2, 1)$, $f(2) = 2(2) - 3 = 1$, which matches the second coordinate. It lies on the line.
Testing $(3, 2)$ the same way gives $f(3) = 3$, not $2$.

flags.text: No caution box or wrong option was supplied. The only usable evidence is the remark about f(x)=ax passing through the origin. The entry is an inference from that remark, not a printed book error.
I wrote no entries for constant functions, for plotting points without joining them, or for confusing linear with quadratic. The evidence did not support any of these as a diagnosable error.

entries.label: Maximum and minimum exchanged
entries.description: Reads the sign of a the wrong way: a < 0 opens downward and gives a maximum.
entries.signal: The answer names a minimum where the curve opens downward, or the reverse.

refutation.text_md: Your value is right — the issue is what to call it.
In $f(x) = -x^2 + 4x - 1$ the coefficient of $x^2$ is negative, so the parabola opens DOWNWARD and the vertex is the highest point: a maximum.
$a > 0$ opens upward and gives a minimum; $a < 0$ opens downward and gives a maximum.

entries.label: The sign of $a$ not read as the direction the parabola opens
entries.description: Sketches $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ curving the opposite way, having treated the sign of $a$ as affecting only position.
entries.signal: The drawn curve's turning point is a minimum where the true one is a maximum, or the reverse.

refutation.text_md: The shape is right — that is a parabola, and it turns where a parabola should.
It opens the wrong way, and the sign of $a$ is the whole story: $a > 0$ opens upwards, $a < 0$ opens downwards.
The reason is worth one line: for large $|x|$ the $ax^2$ term drowns out the rest, and $x^2$ is always positive — so the tail follows the sign of $a$.
Read the sign of $a$ before drawing anything, and you have the direction for free.

entries.label: Constant term read as the extreme value
entries.description: Reports c as the maximum or minimum instead of evaluating f at the vertex.
entries.signal: The stated extreme value equals the constant term.

refutation.text_md: $-1$ is in the function, so it is a reasonable thing to reach for.
But $c$ is the value at $x = 0$, not at the vertex. The vertex is at $x = -\frac{b}{2a} = 2$, and $f(2) = -4 + 8 - 1 = 3$.
Find the vertex's $x$ first, then substitute to get the extreme value.
